questions.question: Describe the journey and working conditions in a deep gold mine.
questions.expected_answer: Miners collect lamps and equipment and ride a fast steel cage down the shaft, sometimes changing shafts, then walk or take a train through tunnels; the journey can take an hour or more. Deep mines reach about four kilometres down. They work in stopes, which are low because the gold reef is thin, often kneeling or lying down, in darkness lit only by cap lamps, with loud noise.

questions.question: Explain why ventilation and cooling are needed and how they work.
questions.expected_answer: The deeper the mine, the hotter the rock, up to about sixty degrees Celsius, which can cause heatstroke. Miners also need fresh air, and heat, dust, fumes and gases must be removed. Huge surface fans pull used air out through ventilation shafts, drawing fresh air down others. Refrigeration plants chill water to cool the air, and some mines send ice down.

questions.question: Describe the dangers of rock falls and dust and how they are reduced.
questions.expected_answer: The weight of rock above presses on tunnels, causing rock falls and sudden rockbursts. Miners support rock with steel props, wooden packs, rock bolts and mesh, and tap the roof to check for loose rock. Drilling and blasting make silica dust, which can cause silicosis and increase TB risk, so water is sprayed and miners wear dust masks.
